drills.q: Someone says 'we deployed it on SageMaker.' What's your immediate follow-up question and why does it matter?
drills.a: Which inference product specifically — Real-Time Endpoint, Serverless, Async, or Batch Transform. Each has a completely different cost model and latency profile, so the answer changes the entire cost/latency conversation.

drills.q: A workload has bursty, unpredictable traffic averaging 50 requests/hour. Real-Time Endpoint or Serverless Inference?
drills.a: Serverless Inference — it scales to zero and bills per invocation, avoiding paying for an always-on instance serving mostly idle time; accept the 1-5s cold start tradeoff for infrequent bursts.

drills.q: Explain in one sentence why Bedrock and self-hosting have structurally different cost curves as volume grows.
drills.a: Bedrock's cost is linear in tokens processed (pay only for usage), while self-hosting's cost is a step function in provisioned instance-hours (pay for capacity whether it's used or idle), so self-hosting's effective per-token cost falls as utilization rises toward the linear Bedrock rate and below it.

drills.q: Design the serving path for a workload doing 500K requests/day with steady, predictable traffic and a loose 2-second internal SLA. Justify the choice.
drills.a: Self-hosted vLLM on EC2/EKS sized to steady-state throughput with modest autoscaling headroom — 500K req/day steady traffic is well above typical self-hosting crossover estimates, and the loose SLA is easily met, so unit economics favor self-hosting over Bedrock on-demand at this volume.

drills.q: Your team's Bedrock bill tripled with no increase in request volume. Walk through your diagnosis in order.
drills.a: 1) Check token counts per request per prompt-template version first — a context-length regression is the most common invisible cause. 2) Check for a fallback path silently routing to a pricier model tier. 3) Check for unintended Priority-tier usage. 4) Check for an unpinned model alias resolving to a different-priced model version.

drills.q: A compliance team says 'no third-party process may touch our data, even within our own cloud account.' Does Bedrock or SageMaker satisfy this?
drills.a: Neither, under that literal wording — both are AWS-operated managed services running within the customer's account boundary, but AWS's compute is still the entity processing the data. Only genuinely self-hosted infrastructure the organization directly controls end-to-end satisfies that specific requirement.

drills.q: Your team signed a 6-month Bedrock Provisioned Throughput commitment and traffic has since grown 3x, hitting the reserved capacity ceiling. What are your options?
drills.a: Purchase additional model units (a new/expanded commitment), or overflow excess traffic to on-demand as a burst valve. Provisioned throughput isn't automatically elastic, so an overflow path should be designed in from the start rather than assumed.

drills.q: A team wants to self-host for cost reasons but the task requires frontier-model reasoning quality that no open-weight model currently matches. How do you respond?
drills.a: The cost arithmetic is moot if no self-hostable model meets the quality bar — recommend staying on the hosted API and revisiting self-hosting once open-weight model quality closes the gap, rather than degrading product quality to chase infrastructure savings.

drills.q: Leadership asks for a cost comparison between Bedrock and self-hosting, but only gives you total monthly spend, not usage data. What do you ask for before running any numbers?
drills.a: Requests/day, average input/output token length distribution, and traffic steadiness (peak-to-average ratio) — the crossover point depends heavily on all three, and total spend alone can't distinguish a high-volume-cheap-token workload from a low-volume-expensive-token one.

drills.q: A team already runs EKS comfortably for other services and needs a fine-tuned open-weight model not on Bedrock. Do you recommend SageMaker or plain self-hosted EKS, and why?
drills.a: Plain self-hosted EKS — since the team already has mature Kubernetes tooling and on-call practices, SageMaker's abstraction adds AWS-specific configuration surface without adding capability they don't already have, and avoids introducing a second, SageMaker-specific operational paradigm alongside the existing stack.

drills.q: Present the case for migrating an existing Bedrock product to self-hosted, addressing both cost and risk, in a form a non-technical leader could act on.
drills.a: State the scale-relative-to-crossover finding plainly (e.g. 'we're at Nx the estimated crossover volume, self-hosting likely saves $Y/month net of ops cost'), and name the migration risk explicitly if models differ (re-validating quality against an open-weight alternative is a real evaluation project, estimated at Z weeks) rather than hedging with 'it depends' and no conclusion.
